title: Ὀδυσσεὺς ἱκέτης
titleEn: The Suppliant in the Hall — Odyssey 7.133–239
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Odysseus, still wrapped in the mist Athena poured round him, crosses the threshold of the Phaeacian palace, finds the leaders pouring their last libation of the evening, and reaches Queen Arete and King Alcinous. He throws his arms round the queen’s knees, the mist falls away, and the company is struck dumb. He prays for their prosperity and asks for a passage home, then sits down in the ashes of the hearth. After a long silence the old hero Echeneus tells Alcinous that it is not fitting to leave a stranger there; Alcinous raises him to a shining chair, food and water are brought, and a libation is poured to Zeus, the protector of suppliants. Alcinous promises a sacrifice and a passage for the morning and wonders whether the stranger may be a god. Odysseus answers that he is a mortal, begs to be allowed to eat before he tells his troubles, and asks only for a passage at dawn. When the others have gone to bed, Arete, who knows the cloak and tunic he is wearing, asks him who he is and who gave him the clothes.

sentences.t: ἔνθα στὰς θηεῖτο πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς.
sentences.tr: entha stas thēeito polytlas dios Odysseus.
sentences.l: There, standing, he gazed, much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus.
sentences.i: There he stood and gazed, much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus.
sentences.n: ἔνθα ‘there’ points to the threshold of the palace, which he crosses in the next line. θηεῖτο is the imperfect of θηέομαι ‘gaze at in wonder’ (Attic θεάομαι), and στάς is the aorist participle of ἵστημι, ‘having stopped’. πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς is a fixed name-formula that closes the line; both epithets are translated every time it comes. πολύτλας is built on τλάω ‘endure’, so ‘much-enduring’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ δὴ πάντα ἑῷ θηήσατο θυμῷ,
καρπαλίμως ὑπὲρ οὐδὸν ἐβήσετο δώματος εἴσω.
sentences.tr:
autar epei dē panta heōi thēēsato thymōi,
karpalimōs hyper oudon ebēseto dōmatos eisō.
sentences.l:
But when indeed all things in his own heart he had wondered at,
quickly over the threshold he stepped, into the house within.
sentences.i: But when he had taken in the whole sight to his heart’s content, he quickly stepped over the threshold into the house.
sentences.n: ἑῷ is the possessive ‘his own’ (ὅς, ἥ, ὅν), not the relative; ἑῷ θυμῷ is ‘in his own heart’. θηήσατο is the aorist of the same verb as θηεῖτο, with Ionic η where Attic has α. ἐβήσετο is an epic aorist of βαίνω, ‘he stepped’. ὑπὲρ οὐδόν is ‘over the threshold’, and εἴσω ‘inside’ takes the genitive δώματος: ‘into the house’. Odysseus is still unseen at this point.

sentences.t:
εὗρε δὲ Φαιήκων ἡγήτορας ἠδὲ μέδοντας
σπένδοντας δεπάεσσιν ἐυσκόπῳ ἀργεϊφόντῃ,
ᾧ πυμάτῳ σπένδεσκον, ὅτε μνησαίατο κοίτου.
sentences.tr:
heure de Phaiēkōn hēgētoras ēde medontas
spendontas depaessin eyskopōi argeïphontēi,
hōi pymatōi spendeskon, hote mnēsaiato koitou.
sentences.l:
And he found the Phaeacians’ leaders and lords
pouring libations from cups to keen-sighted Argeïphontes,
to whom last they used to pour, whenever they had bed in mind.
sentences.i: There he found the leaders and lords of the Phaeacians pouring libations from their cups to the keen-sighted slayer of Argus, the god to whom they poured last, whenever they were thinking of bed.
sentences.n: Φαιήκων ἡγήτορας ἠδὲ μέδοντας is a formula, ‘leaders and lords of the Phaeacians’. δεπάεσσιν is a dative plural in -εσσι(ν). ἐύσκοπος is ‘keen-sighted’. ἀργεϊφόντης is a name of Hermes whose meaning is disputed: the ancient explanation ‘slayer of Argus’ is followed in the English but is not known to be right. σπένδεσκον has the iterative ending -εσκ-, ‘used to pour’, and μνησαίατο is an optative in a ‘whenever’ clause: ‘whenever they thought of’, with κοίτου in the genitive. So the last libation before bed goes to Hermes.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὁ βῆ διὰ δῶμα πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεὺς
πολλὴν ἠέρ’ ἔχων, ἥν οἱ περίχευεν Ἀθήνη,
ὄφρ’ ἵκετ’ Ἀρήτην τε καὶ Ἀλκίνοον βασιλῆα.
sentences.tr:
autar ho bē dia dōma polytlas dios Odysseus
pollēn ēer’ echōn, hēn hoi pericheuen Athēnē,
ophr’ hiket’ Arētēn te kai Alkinoon basilēa.
sentences.l:
But he went through the house, much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus,
holding much mist, which about him Athena had poured,
until he came to Arete and to Alcinous the king.
sentences.i: But he made his way through the house, much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus, wrapped in a thick mist that Athena had poured about him, until he came to Arete and King Alcinous.
sentences.n: βῆ is the unaugmented root aorist of βαίνω, ‘went’. πολλὴν ἠέρα ἔχων is ‘holding much mist’: Athena’s mist hides him as he walks through the hall. οἱ in ἥν οἱ περίχευεν is the dative pronoun ‘about him’; ὄφρα means ‘until’, and ἵκετο is the epic ‘came to’. The queen is named first, before the king: the next lines show why, since it is Arete’s knees he clasps.

sentences.t:
ἀμφὶ δ’ ἄρ’ Ἀρήτης βάλε γούνασι χεῖρας Ὀδυσσεύς,
καὶ τότε δή ῥ’ αὐτοῖο πάλιν χύτο θέσφατος ἀήρ.
sentences.tr:
amphi d’ ar’ Arētēs bale gounasi cheiras Odysseus,
kai tote dē rh’ autoio palin chyto thesphatos aēr.
sentences.l:
And around Arete he threw, at her knees, his hands, Odysseus,
and then indeed the god-declared mist was poured back from him.
sentences.i: He threw his hands round Arete, at her knees, Odysseus, and just then the god-decreed mist was poured away from him.
sentences.n: ἀμφὶ … βάλε is tmesis, ‘threw round’, and Ἀρήτης is genitive with it: ‘round Arete’, with γούνασι ‘at her knees’, the suppliant’s hold. χύτο is an unaugmented aorist of χέω, ‘was poured’. ἀήρ is the same word as ἠήρ, whose accusative ἠέρ’ stands in 140, both ‘mist’. θέσφατος is ‘god-declared’, from θεός and φημί; the sense of the compound as said of a mist is not certain, ‘decreed by the gods’ is the usual gloss. The mist goes as soon as he touches her.

sentences.t: οἱ δ’ ἄνεῳ ἐγένοντο, δόμον κάτα φῶτα ἰδόντες·
sentences.tr: hoi d’ aneōi egenonto, domon kata phōta idontes·
sentences.l: And they became speechless, throughout the house, the man seeing;
sentences.i: All through the house they fell speechless at the sight of the man;
sentences.n: οἱ here is the article as a pronoun, nominative plural ‘they’ (not the dative singular οἱ of line 140). ἄνεῳ is the masculine nominative plural of ἄνεως, ‘speechless, struck dumb’. δόμον κάτα is κατὰ δόμον with the preposition placed after its noun, and the accent thrown back: ‘through the house’. φῶτα is the accusative of φώς ‘man’, object of the participle ἰδόντες.

sentences.t: θαύμαζον δ’ ὁρόωντες.
sentences.tr: thaumazon d’ horoōntes.
sentences.l: and they marvelled, looking.
sentences.i: They gazed at him in wonder.
sentences.n: θαύμαζον is the imperfect of θαυμάζω ‘wonder at’, the imperfect giving the lasting state. ὁρόωντες is the uncontracted participle of ὁράω ‘look’, with the vowels left open (Attic ὁρῶντες). The sentence stops in the middle of the line: the Greek has a full stop after ὁρόωντες, and a new sentence starts within the same line.

sentences.t: ὁ δὲ λιτάνευεν Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.tr: ho de litaneuen Odysseus·
sentences.l: and he besought them, Odysseus:
sentences.i: and Odysseus made his entreaty:
sentences.n: ὁ is the pronoun ‘he’ (not an article), with δέ ‘and, but’. λιτάνευεν is the imperfect of λιτανεύω ‘entreat, beseech’, from λιτή ‘prayer’; it is the word for what a suppliant does. The ano teleia (·) at the end announces the speech, which Odysseus begins with a vocative in the next line.

sentences.t:
Ἀρήτη, θύγατερ Ῥηξήνορος ἀντιθέοιο,
σόν τε πόσιν σά τε γούναθ’ ἱκάνω πολλὰ μογήσας
τούσδε τε δαιτυμόνας·
sentences.tr:
Arētē, thygater Rhēxēnoros antitheoio,
son te posin sa te gounath’ hikanō polla mogēsas
tousde te daitymonas·
sentences.i: “Arete, daughter of godlike Rhexenor, I come to your husband and to your knees, after much toil, and to these banqueters as well;
sentences.n: Ῥηξήνορος ἀντιθέοιο is ‘of godlike Rhexenor’, the queen’s father, the epithet ἀντιθέοιο being a genitive in -οιο (Attic -ου) and ἀντίθεος the table’s ‘godlike’. The verb ἱκάνω ‘I come to, approach’ comes late, after its objects: σόν τε πόσιν σά τε γούναθ’ ‘both your husband and your knees’, and τούσδε τε δαιτυμόνας, ‘these banqueters’. γούναθ’ is γούνατα with its final vowel elided. πολλὰ μογήσας is ‘having toiled much’, the aorist participle of μογέω.

sentences.t:
τοῖσιν θεοὶ ὄλβια δοῖεν
ζωέμεναι, καὶ παισὶν ἐπιτρέψειεν ἕκαστος
κτήματ’ ἐνὶ μεγάροισι γέρας θ’ ὅ τι δῆμος ἔδωκεν·
sentences.tr:
toisin theoi olbia doien
zōemenai, kai paisin epitrepseien hekastos
ktēmat’ eni megaroisi geras th’ ho ti dēmos edōken·
sentences.i: may the gods grant them to live in happiness, and may each of them hand on to his children the possessions in his halls and whatever honour the people gave him;
sentences.n: τοῖσιν is ‘to them’, the banqueters. δοῖεν and ἐπιτρέψειεν are aorist optatives of wish, ‘may they grant’, ‘may he hand over’. ζωέμεναι is the epic infinitive of ζώω ‘live’ (Attic ζῆν) in the -έμεναι ending; ὄλβια, ‘blessed things’, is what the gods are asked to grant, and ζωέμεναι says to what end: ‘to live in blessedness’. ἕκαστος ‘each one’ is singular. γέρας is ‘honour, privilege’, and ὅ τι is ‘whatever’, two words. The dative endings -οισι(ν) and -ῃσι(ν) recur in this passage.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐμοὶ πομπὴν ὀτρύνετε πατρίδ’ ἱκέσθαι
θᾶσσον, ἐπεὶ δὴ δηθὰ φίλων ἄπο πήματα πάσχω.
sentences.tr:
autar emoi pompēn otrynete patrid’ hikesthai
thasson, epei dē dētha philōn apo pēmata paschō.
sentences.l:
But for me a conveyance speed on, to reach my fatherland
sooner, since for long far from my dear ones I suffer woes.”
sentences.i: But speed my conveyance, so that I may reach my fatherland sooner, for I have long suffered woes far from those I love.”
sentences.n: The wish gives way to the request. πομπή ‘sending, conveyance home’ is the thing he asks for, and the word Alcinous takes up at 191–193. ὀτρύνετε is the imperative of ὀτρύνω ‘urge on, speed’, and πατρίδ’ ἱκέσθαι ‘to reach my fatherland’ is an aorist infinitive of purpose. θᾶσσον is the comparative ‘sooner’, and δηθά ‘for a long time’. φίλων ἄπο is ἀπὸ φίλων with the preposition after its noun, so the accent moves back.

sentences.t:
ὣς εἰπὼν κατ’ ἄρ’ ἕζετ’ ἐπ’ ἐσχάρῃ ἐν κονίῃσιν
πὰρ πυρί·
sentences.tr:
hōs eipōn kat’ ar’ hezet’ ep’ escharēi en koniēisin
par pyri·
sentences.l:
So having spoken, down then he sat on the hearth in the ashes
beside the fire;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and sat down on the hearth in the ashes beside the fire;
sentences.n: κατ’ … ἕζετ’ is tmesis for κατέζετο ‘sat down’, with ἄρ’ between preverb and verb; ἕζετο is the imperfect of ἕζομαι ‘sit’. ἐσχάρῃ is the hearth, and κονίῃσιν, a plural dative in -ῃσιν, is the dust or ashes on it. He sits where a suppliant sits, and it is this seat that Echeneus objects to in 160. ὣς εἰπών is ‘so having spoken’.

sentences.t: οἱ δ’ ἄρα πάντες ἀκὴν ἐγένοντο σιωπῇ.
sentences.tr: hoi d’ ara pantes akēn egenonto siōpēi.
sentences.l: and they then all became still in silence.
sentences.i: and all the rest fell hushed and silent.
sentences.n: οἱ is again the pronoun ‘they’, the company. ἀκήν is an adverb ‘hushed, in silence’ and σιωπῇ is a dative ‘in silence’; the two together give a doubled emphasis, ‘still, in silence’. The previous sentence ends at the ano teleia after πὰρ πυρί, early in this line, and this sentence begins in the same line.

sentences.t:
ὀψὲ δὲ δὴ μετέειπε γέρων ἥρως Ἐχένηος,
ὃς δὴ Φαιήκων ἀνδρῶν προγενέστερος ἦεν
καὶ μύθοισι κέκαστο, παλαιά τε πολλά τε εἰδώς·
sentences.tr:
opse de dē meteeipe gerōn hērōs Echenēos,
hos dē Phaiēkōn andrōn progenesteros ēen
kai mythoisi kekasto, palaia te polla te eidōs·
sentences.i: Then at last the old hero Echeneus spoke among them, the elder of the Phaeacian men, who excelled in speech and knew many things from long ago;
sentences.n: ὀψέ ‘late’ tells us the silence has gone on a while. μετέειπε is ‘spoke among (them)’. γέρων ἥρως is ‘old hero’: ἥρως is a title of honour for a man of standing, here an elder, and is translated ‘hero’ every time. Ἐχένηος is Ionic for Ἐχένεως. προγενέστερος is ‘born earlier, older’, with the genitive Φαιήκων ἀνδρῶν. κέκαστο is the pluperfect of καίνυμαι ‘excel’, with the dative μύθοισι ‘in words’, and εἰδώς the participle of οἶδα, ‘knowing’.

sentences.t: ὅ σφιν ἐὺ φρονέων ἀγορήσατο καὶ μετέειπεν·
sentences.tr: ho sphin ey phroneōn agorēsato kai meteeipen·
sentences.l: he, well-disposed in mind toward them, addressed-the-assembly and spoke among them:
sentences.i: with kindly intent toward them he addressed the assembly and spoke among them:
sentences.n: ὅ is the pronoun ‘he’, and σφιν is ‘to them’ (epic dative plural of the third-person pronoun). ἐὺ φρονέων is ‘thinking well’, hence ‘well-disposed’. ἀγορήσατο καὶ μετέειπεν ‘addressed the assembly and spoke among them’ is a stock pair, the first verb from ἀγοράομαι ‘speak in assembly’, the second ‘spoke among’. The line is a speech-introduction, and the same pair of verbs comes again before Alcinous speaks (185).

sentences.t:
Ἀλκίνο’, οὐ μέν τοι τόδε κάλλιον, οὐδὲ ἔοικε,
ξεῖνον μὲν χαμαὶ ἧσθαι ἐπ’ ἐσχάρῃ ἐν κονίῃσιν,
οἵδε δὲ σὸν μῦθον ποτιδέγμενοι ἰσχανόωνται.
sentences.tr:
Alkino’, ou men toi tode kallion, oude eoike,
xeinon men chamai hēsthai ep’ escharēi en koniēisin,
hoide de son mython potidegmenoi ischanoōntai.
sentences.l:
“Alcinous, this is not indeed the finer way, nor is it fitting,
that a stranger on the ground sits at the hearth in the ashes,
while these hold back, waiting for your word.
sentences.i: “Alcinous, this is surely not the finer thing, nor is it fitting, that a stranger should sit on the ground at the hearth in the ashes, while these men hold back, waiting for your word.
sentences.n: The sentence is built on the pair ξεῖνον μὲν … οἵδε δέ, the stranger in the ashes set against the men who hold back, waiting. ἔοικε is the perfect of ἔοικα used impersonally, ‘it is fitting’, with the infinitive ἧσθαι ‘to sit’. κάλλιον is the comparative of καλός. οὐ μέν τοι is ‘not indeed’. ποτιδέγμενοι is epic ποτί for πρός, ‘waiting for’. ἰσχανόωνται is the open form (diectasis) of ἰσχανάομαι ‘hold oneself back’.

sentences.t:
ἄλλ’ ἄγε δὴ ξεῖνον μὲν ἐπὶ θρόνου ἀργυροήλου
εἷσον ἀναστήσας, σὺ δὲ κηρύκεσσι κέλευσον
οἶνον ἐπικρῆσαι, ἵνα καὶ Διὶ τερπικεραύνῳ
σπείσομεν, ὅς θ’ ἱκέτῃσιν ἅμ’ αἰδοίοισιν ὀπηδεῖ·
sentences.tr:
all’ age dē xeinon men epi thronou argyroēlou
heison anastēsas, sy de kērykessi keleuson
oinon epikrēsai, hina kai Dii terpikeraunōi
speisomen, hos th’ hiketēisin ham’ aidoioisin opēdei·
sentences.l:
But come now, the stranger upon a silver-studded chair
seat, having raised him up, and you, to the heralds give the order
to mix wine, so that also to bolt-delighting Zeus
we may pour, who keeps company with revered suppliants;
sentences.i: But come now: raise the stranger up and seat him on a silver-studded chair, and you, tell the heralds to mix wine, so that we may pour a libation also to Zeus, who delights in the thunderbolt and keeps company with revered suppliants;
sentences.n: εἷσον is the aorist imperative of ἵζω ‘seat’, with ἀναστήσας ‘having made him rise’. ἀργυροήλου is ‘silver-studded’, from ἧλος ‘nail, stud’. κηρύκεσσι is a dative in -εσσι, and ἐπικρῆσαι is ‘to mix’, wine with water, as at a feast. σπείσομεν is a short-vowel subjunctive after ἵνα, ‘that we may pour’. τερπικέραυνος is ‘delighting in the thunderbolt’. ὅς θ’ has the epic τε of general statement: Zeus is, always, the companion of suppliants. Zeus as protector of suppliants is the reason given for the libation.

sentences.t: δόρπον δὲ ξείνῳ ταμίη δότω ἔνδον ἐόντων.
sentences.tr: dorpon de xeinōi tamiē dotō endon eontōn.
sentences.l: and supper for the stranger let the housekeeper give, of what is within.”
sentences.i: and let the housekeeper give the stranger his supper from what is in the house.”
sentences.n: ταμίη is the housekeeper, who brings the food at 175. δότω is the third-person imperative of δίδωμι, ‘let her give’. ξείνῳ is the epic spelling of ξένῳ, ‘to the stranger’. ἔνδον ἐόντων is a genitive of the whole, ‘of the things being inside’, that is, of what is in the store; ἐόντων is the epic participle (Attic ὄντων). δόρπον ‘supper’ is the word from which δορπῆσαι in 215 is made.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ τό γ’ ἄκουσ’ ἱερὸν μένος Ἀλκινόοιο,
χειρὸς ἑλὼν Ὀδυσῆα δαΐφρονα ποικιλομήτην
ὦρσεν ἀπ’ ἐσχαρόφιν καὶ ἐπὶ θρόνου εἷσε φαεινοῦ,
sentences.tr:
autar epei to g’ akous’ hieron menos Alkinooio,
cheiros helōn Odysēa daïphrona poikilomētēn
ōrsen ap’ escharophin kai epi thronou heise phaeinou,
sentences.l:
But when this heard the sacred strength of Alcinous,
by the hand taking Odysseus, wise-minded, of many-colored cunning,
he raised him from the hearth and on a shining chair sat him,
sentences.i: But when the sacred strength of Alcinous heard this, he took Odysseus, wise-hearted and full of shifting cunning, by the hand, raised him from the hearth and seated him on a shining chair,
sentences.n: ἱερὸν μένος Ἀλκινόοιο is a periphrasis: ‘the sacred strength of Alcinous’ stands where the plain name could have been, and the English keeps it. τό γ’ is ‘this’, the article as pronoun, and ἄκουσ’ is ἄκουσε. δαΐφρων is ‘wise-minded’ on the reading from δαῆναι ‘learn, know’; the other ancient derivation, from δάϊος ‘hostile’, would make it ‘warlike’. ποικιλομήτης is ‘of varied, many-coloured cunning’ (ποικίλος, μῆτις). ὦρσεν is the aorist of ὄρνυμι ‘raise’, with the augment (ὄρ- → ὦρ-), and ἐσχαρόφιν has the -φιν ending ‘from the hearth’.

sentences.t:
υἱὸν ἀναστήσας ἀγαπήνορα Λαοδάμαντα,
ὅς οἱ πλησίον ἷζε, μάλιστα δέ μιν φιλέεσκεν.
sentences.tr:
huion anastēsas agapēnora Laodamanta,
hos hoi plēsion hize, malista de min phileesken.
sentences.l:
his son having made rise, the man-cherishing Laodamas,
who beside him sat, and most of all him used to love.
sentences.i: making his son Laodamas, who prized manliness, get up from where he sat beside him, the son he loved best of all.
sentences.n: The son is made to give up his seat to the guest. ἀγαπήνωρ is built from ἀγαπάω ‘cherish’ and ἀνήρ ‘man’, and its exact sense is not known: ‘loving manliness’ or ‘held dear by men’ are both proposed; the literal line keeps the two parts and the prose takes the first. οἱ is ‘beside him’ (dative), and μιν is ‘him’, that is Laodamas. ἷζε is ‘sat’, from ἵζω, and φιλέεσκεν has the iterative -εσκ- and the open vowels of φιλέω: ‘used to love’.

sentences.t:
χέρνιβα δ’ ἀμφίπολος προχόῳ ἐπέχευε φέρουσα
καλῇ χρυσείῃ ὑπὲρ ἀργυρέοιο λέβητος,
νίψασθαι·
sentences.tr:
cherniba d’ amphipolos prochoōi epecheue pherousa
kalēi chryseiēi hyper argyreoio lebētos,
nipsasthai·
sentences.i: A handmaid brought water for the hands in a fine golden pitcher and poured it over a silver basin, for them to wash;
sentences.n: This is the customary washing of hands before a meal. χέρνιβα is ‘water for the hands’, brought by an ἀμφίπολος ‘handmaid’ in a προχόος, a pitcher, and poured ὑπὲρ … λέβητος ‘over a basin’. καλῇ χρυσείῃ are feminine datives in -ῃ, ‘fine golden’, agreeing with the pitcher. νίψασθαι is an infinitive of purpose, ‘for washing (the hands)’. φέρουσα ‘bringing’ is a present participle.

sentences.t: παρὰ δὲ ξεστὴν ἐτάνυσσε τράπεζαν.
sentences.tr: para de xestēn etanysse trapezan.
sentences.l: and beside them she drew up a polished table.
sentences.i: and she drew a polished table up beside them.
sentences.n: παρά is an adverb ‘alongside’ standing apart from its verb, and the same handmaid is still the subject. ἐτάνυσσε is the aorist of τανύω ‘stretch, spread’. ξεστήν is ‘polished, smoothed’, from ξέω ‘scrape smooth’; the table is the surface on which the food is laid at once.

sentences.t:
σῖτον δ’ αἰδοίη ταμίη παρέθηκε φέρουσα,
εἴδατα πόλλ’ ἐπιθεῖσα, χαριζομένη παρεόντων.
sentences.tr:
siton d’ aidoiē tamiē parethēke pherousa,
eidata poll’ epitheisa, charizomenē pareontōn.
sentences.l:
And bread a revered housekeeper set beside them, bringing it,
and laid on many dishes, giving freely of what was at hand;
sentences.i: A revered housekeeper brought bread and set it beside them, and laid on many dishes, giving freely of what she had by her;
sentences.n: αἰδοίη ταμίη is a stock pair, ‘a revered housekeeper’, translated the same each time. σῖτον is ‘bread, food’. παρέθηκε is the aorist of παρατίθημι ‘set beside’, and ἐπιθεῖσα the aorist participle of ἐπιτίθημι ‘laid on’; χαριζομένη is ‘giving freely’. παρεόντων is a genitive of the whole with the open vowels of the epic participle: ‘of the things that were at hand’. The housekeeper is the one Echeneus called on at 166.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ὁ πῖνε καὶ ἦσθε πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς.
sentences.tr: autar ho pine kai ēsthe polytlas dios Odysseus.
sentences.l: And he drank and ate, much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus.
sentences.i: And he drank and ate, much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus.
sentences.n: ἦσθε is the imperfect of ἔσθω ‘eat’ (Attic ἤσθιε). It must not be taken for a form of ἧμαι ‘sit’, as ἧσθαι in line 160 is. πῖνε ‘drank’ is the imperfect of πίνω. αὐτὰρ ὁ is ‘and he’, turning back to Odysseus after the servants; ὁ is the pronoun. The name-formula returns, with both epithets.

sentences.t: καὶ τότε κήρυκα προσέφη μένος Ἀλκινόοιο·
sentences.tr: kai tote kēryka prosephē menos Alkinooio·
sentences.l: And then to the herald addressed the strength of Alcinous:
sentences.i: Then the strength of Alcinous spoke to the herald:
sentences.n: μένος Ἀλκινόοιο is the same periphrasis as in 167, now without ἱερόν ‘sacred’: ‘the strength of Alcinous’ is Alcinous himself. κήρυκα is the accusative of the person addressed, with προσέφη ‘addressed’, the aorist of πρόσφημι. The herald is named in the vocative in the next line.

sentences.t:
Ποντόνοε, κρητῆρα κερασσάμενος μέθυ νεῖμον
πᾶσιν ἀνὰ μέγαρον, ἵνα καὶ Διὶ τερπικεραύνῳ
σπείσομεν, ὅς θ’ ἱκέτῃσιν ἅμ’ αἰδοίοισιν ὀπηδεῖ.
sentences.tr:
Pontonoe, krētēra kerassamenos methy neimon
pasin ana megaron, hina kai Dii terpikeraunōi
speisomen, hos th’ hiketēisin ham’ aidoioisin opēdei.
sentences.l:
“Pontonous, a mixing-bowl having mixed, wine distribute
to all throughout the hall, so that also to bolt-delighting Zeus
we may pour, who keeps company with revered suppliants.”
sentences.i: “Pontonous, mix a bowl of wine and serve it to everyone throughout the hall, so that we may pour a libation also to Zeus, who delights in the thunderbolt and keeps company with revered suppliants.”
sentences.n: Ποντόνοε is the vocative of Ποντόνοος, the herald. κρητῆρα κερασσάμενος is ‘having mixed a mixing-bowl’, the bowl in which wine was mixed with water, and μέθυ is ‘wine’. νεῖμον is the aorist imperative of νέμω ‘distribute’. The second half of 180 and all of 181 repeat Echeneus’s words in 164–165, so Alcinous takes up his advice in his own words, and the English repeats too.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, Ποντόνοος δὲ μελίφρονα οἶνον ἐκίρνα,
νώμησεν δ’ ἄρα πᾶσιν ἐπαρξάμενος δεπάεσσιν.
sentences.tr:
hōs phato, Pontonoos de meliphrona oinon ekirna,
nōmēsen d’ ara pasin eparxamenos depaessin.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and Pontonous the honey-hearted wine mixed,
and dealt it out then to all, having first poured drops into the cups.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Pontonous mixed the heart-sweetening wine and served it out to all, first pouring a few drops into each cup.
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο is ‘so he spoke’. μελίφρων is from μέλι ‘honey’ and φρήν ‘heart, mind’; said of wine, ‘sweet to the heart’ is the usual sense, but the exact meaning is not known, so the literal line keeps the parts. ἐκίρνα is the imperfect of κίρνημι ‘mix’ (= κεράννυμι), and νώμησεν the aorist of νωμάω ‘deal out’. ἐπαρξάμενος δεπάεσσιν is the ritual first pouring, usually taken as ‘having poured the first drops into the cups’; the detail is not certain.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ σπεῖσάν τ’ ἔπιόν θ’, ὅσον ἤθελε θυμός,
τοῖσιν δ’ Ἀλκίνοος ἀγορήσατο καὶ μετέειπε·
sentences.tr:
autar epei speisan t’ epion th’, hoson ēthele thymos,
toisin d’ Alkinoos agorēsato kai meteeipe·
sentences.l:
But when they had poured libations and drunk, as much as their heart wished,
to them Alcinous addressed-the-assembly and spoke among them:
sentences.i: But when they had poured libations and drunk as much as their hearts wished, Alcinous addressed the assembly and spoke among them:
sentences.n: The first line is a stock line that closes a meal’s drinking. ἤθελε is the imperfect of ἐθέλω ‘wish’ and θυμός, ‘heart’, is the seat of appetite, so ‘as much as their heart wished’. τοῖσιν is a dative in -οισιν, ‘to them’, the guests. ἀγορήσατο καὶ μετέειπε is the same pair of verbs as in 158, ‘addressed the assembly and spoke among them’.

sentences.t:
κέκλυτε, Φαιήκων ἡγήτορες ἠδὲ μέδοντες
ὄφρ’ εἴπω τά με θυμὸς ἐνὶ στήθεσσι κελεύει.
sentences.tr:
keklyte, Phaiēkōn hēgētores ēde medontes
ophr’ eipō ta me thymos eni stēthessi keleuei.
sentences.l:
“Hear me, leaders and lords of the Phaeacians,
that I may say what my heart in my breast bids.
sentences.i: “Hear me, leaders and lords of the Phaeacians, so that I may say what the heart in my breast bids me say.
sentences.n: κέκλυτε is the reduplicated aorist imperative of κλύω, an emphatic ‘hear!’. Φαιήκων ἡγήτορες ἠδὲ μέδοντες is the formula of line 136, ‘leaders and lords of the Phaeacians’, now in the vocative. ὄφρ’ εἴπω is a purpose clause with the aorist subjunctive, ‘so that I may say’. τά με is the article as relative pronoun, ‘the things that … me’. στήθεσσι is a dative in -εσσι, ‘in my breast’.

sentences.t: νῦν μὲν δαισάμενοι κατακείετε οἴκαδ’ ἰόντες·
sentences.tr: nyn men daisamenoi katakeiete oikad’ iontes·
sentences.l: Now, having feasted, lie down, going home;
sentences.i: Now that you have feasted, go home and lie down;
sentences.n: νῦν μέν sets tonight against ἠῶθεν δέ ‘but at dawn’ in the next line. δαισάμενοι is the aorist middle participle of δαίνυμι ‘feast’. κατακείετε is a present imperative ‘lie down, go to bed’ (an epic form from κεῖμαι). οἴκαδ’ is οἴκαδε, ‘homewards’, with -δε marking direction, and ἰόντες ‘going’ is a present participle.

sentences.t:
ἠῶθεν δὲ γέροντας ἐπὶ πλέονας καλέσαντες
ξεῖνον ἐνὶ μεγάροις ξεινίσσομεν ἠδὲ θεοῖσιν
ῥέξομεν ἱερὰ καλά,
sentences.tr:
ēōthen de gerontas epi pleonas kalesantes
xeinon eni megarois xeinissomen ēde theoisin
rhexomen hiera kala,
sentences.l:
and at dawn, elders in greater number having called,
the stranger in our halls we will entertain, and to the gods
we will offer fine sacrifices,
sentences.i: and at dawn, when we have called in more of the elders, we shall entertain the stranger in our halls and offer fine sacrifices to the gods,
sentences.n: ἠῶθεν is ‘at dawn, from dawn’, with -θεν. γέροντας ἐπὶ πλέονας is ‘still more elders’, more of the older men. ξεινίσσομεν can be read as a future or as a short-vowel subjunctive, ‘let us entertain’; the English takes it as a plain intention, like ῥέξομεν. ῥέξομεν ἱερὰ καλά is ‘we will perform fine sacrifices’. ἐνί is ἐν, and μεγάροις is a dative plural.

sentences.t:
ἔπειτα δὲ καὶ περὶ πομπῆς
μνησόμεθ’, ὥς χ’ ὁ ξεῖνος ἄνευθε πόνου καὶ ἀνίης
πομπῇ ὑφ’ ἡμετέρῃ ἣν πατρίδα γαῖαν ἵκηται
χαίρων καρπαλίμως, εἰ καὶ μάλα τηλόθεν ἐστί,
sentences.tr:
epeita de kai peri pompēs
mnēsometh’, hōs ch’ ho xeinos aneuthe ponou kai aniēs
pompēi hyph’ hēmeterēi hēn patrida gaian hikētai
chairōn karpalimōs, ei kai mala tēlothen esti,
sentences.l:
and then also about a conveyance
we will take thought, how the stranger, without toil and grief,
under our conveyance may reach his own fatherland,
rejoicing, swiftly, even if it is very far away,
sentences.i: and then we shall also consider his passage home, so that the stranger, free of toil and grief, may reach his own fatherland under our escort, rejoicing and swiftly, even if it is very far off,
sentences.n: περὶ πομπῆς is ‘about a conveyance’, the very thing Odysseus asked for. μνησόμεθ’ is ‘we will call to mind, take thought’. ὥς χ’ is ὡς κε (κεν = ἄν), with the subjunctive ἵκηται ‘may reach’, of purpose. ἄνευθε ‘without’ takes the genitive πόνου καὶ ἀνίης. ἣν is the possessive ‘his own’, not the relative. πομπῇ ὑφ’ ἡμετέρῃ is ‘under our escort’, and τηλόθεν ‘from far off’ takes -θεν, so ‘far away’.

sentences.t:
μηδέ τι μεσσηγύς γε κακὸν καὶ πῆμα πάθῃσι,
πρίν γε τὸν ἧς γαίης ἐπιβήμεναι·
sentences.tr:
mēde ti messēgys ge kakon kai pēma pathēisi,
prin ge ton hēs gaiēs epibēmenai·
sentences.l:
and not any evil and woe in between may he suffer,
before he sets foot on his own land;
sentences.i: and suffer no evil or woe on the way, before he sets foot on his own land;
sentences.n: μηδέ … πάθῃσι continues the purpose clause: ‘and may he not suffer’. πάθῃσι is an aorist subjunctive with the -σι ending, Attic πάθῃ. μεσσηγύς is ‘in between, midway’, that is on the journey, and κακὸν καὶ πῆμα ‘evil and woe’ is the pair of nouns. πρίν takes the infinitive, and τὸν … ἐπιβήμεναι is ‘he to set foot’, with the epic infinitive in -μεναι and ἧς the possessive ‘his own’.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα δ’ ἔπειτα
πείσεται, ἅσσα οἱ αἶσα κατὰ κλῶθές τε βαρεῖαι
γιγνομένῳ νήσαντο λίνῳ, ὅτε μιν τέκε μήτηρ.
sentences.tr:
entha d’ epeita
peisetai, hassa hoi aisa kata klōthes te bareiai
gignomenōi nēsanto linōi, hote min teke mētēr.
sentences.l:
and there then
he will suffer whatever his portion and the heavy Spinners
spun for him with the thread, as he was being born, when his mother bore him.
sentences.i: and there, afterwards, he will suffer whatever his portion and the heavy Spinners spun for him with the thread when he was born, when his mother bore him.
sentences.n: ἔνθα δ’ ἔπειτα ‘and there, afterwards’, means once he is home. πείσεται is the future of πάσχω. αἶσα is ‘portion, lot’, and κλῶθες is ‘Spinners’, from κλώθω ‘spin’: the powers who spin each life’s thread at birth, not named or counted here. κατὰ … νήσαντο is tmesis, ‘spun down’. λίνῳ is ‘with the thread’, γιγνομένῳ ‘as he was coming to be’. βαρεῖαι ‘heavy’ agrees with the Spinners.

sentences.t:
εἰ δέ τις ἀθανάτων γε κατ’ οὐρανοῦ εἰλήλουθεν,
ἄλλο τι δὴ τόδ’ ἔπειτα θεοὶ περιμηχανόωνται.
sentences.tr:
ei de tis athanatōn ge kat’ ouranou eilēlouthen,
allo ti dē tod’ epeita theoi perimēchanoōntai.
sentences.l:
But if some one of the immortals has come down from heaven,
then this is some other thing the gods are devising.
sentences.i: But if one of the immortals has come down from heaven, then this is something different that the gods are contriving.
sentences.n: The two lines are one condition: εἰ … εἰλήλουθεν, ‘if he has come’, the perfect of ἔρχομαι, with κατ’ οὐρανοῦ ‘down from heaven’. τις ἀθανάτων is ‘some one of the immortals’, and the Greek does not say he means the stranger; the next lines explain what the gods are said to do. ἄλλο τι is ‘something else’. περιμηχανόωνται is the open form (diectasis) of περιμηχανάομαι ‘contrive’, from μηχανή.

sentences.t:
αἰεὶ γὰρ τὸ πάρος γε θεοὶ φαίνονται ἐναργεῖς
ἡμῖν, εὖτ’ ἔρδωμεν ἀγακλειτὰς ἑκατόμβας,
δαίνυνταί τε παρ’ ἄμμι καθήμενοι ἔνθα περ ἡμεῖς.
sentences.tr:
aiei gar to paros ge theoi phainontai enargeis
hēmin, eut’ erdōmen agakleitas hekatombas,
dainyntai te par’ ammi kathēmenoi entha per hēmeis.
sentences.l:
For always in the past the gods appear manifest
to us, whenever we offer renowned hecatombs,
and feast beside us, sitting just where we do.
sentences.i: For always until now the gods have appeared to us in manifest form, whenever we offer renowned hecatombs, and they feast beside us, sitting just where we sit.
sentences.n: αἰεί ‘always’ is Attic ἀεί, and τὸ πάρος γε ‘hitherto, in the past’. ἐναργεῖς is ‘manifest, in plain sight’. εὖτ’ ἔρδωμεν is a ‘whenever’ clause with the subjunctive, without κε. ἀγακλειτάς is ‘renowned’ (= ἀγακλυτός); a hecatomb is a large sacrifice, literally of a hundred oxen. παρ’ ἄμμι is παρ’ ἡμῖν in the Aeolic form ἄμμι ‘us’, and ἔνθα περ ἡμεῖς ‘just where we (sit)’.

sentences.t:
εἰ δ’ ἄρα τις καὶ μοῦνος ἰὼν ξύμβληται ὁδίτης,
οὔ τι κατακρύπτουσιν, ἐπεί σφισιν ἐγγύθεν εἰμέν,
ὥς περ Κύκλωπές τε καὶ ἄγρια φῦλα Γιγάντων.
sentences.tr:
ei d’ ara tis kai mounos iōn xymblētai hoditēs,
ou ti katakryptousin, epei sphisin engythen eimen,
hōs per Kyklōpes te kai agria phyla Gigantōn.
sentences.l:
But if indeed some traveller, going even alone, meets them,
they in no way hide themselves, since we are near to them,
just as the Cyclopes and the savage tribes of the Giants.”
sentences.i: And if some traveller meets them, even going alone, they do not hide themselves at all, because we are close to them, just as the Cyclopes are, and the savage tribes of the Giants.”
sentences.n: εἰ … ξύμβληται is a general condition, ‘if ever’, the aorist subjunctive of ξυμβάλλω ‘meet’. ὁδίτης is a wayfarer. κατακρύπτουσιν ‘hide’ is the verb with the subject ‘the gods’ understood. ἐγγύθεν εἰμέν is literally ‘we are near’; the Greek does not say near in what way, and the comparison with the Cyclopes and Giants, who are also close to the gods, suggests kinship. ἄγρια is ‘savage’, and ὥς περ ‘just as’.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.tr: ton d’ apameibomenos prosephē polymētis Odysseus·
sentences.l: Him answering addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: In answer Odysseus of many wiles said to him:
sentences.n: τὸν is the pronoun ‘him’. ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη is the reply-formula ‘answering addressed’, made of a participle and a finite verb. πολύμητις is ‘of many wiles’, from πολύς and μῆτις ‘cunning intelligence, craft’, kept apart from πολυμήχανος, which is built on μηχανή ‘device’.

sentences.t: Ἀλκίνο’, ἄλλο τί τοι μελέτω φρεσίν·
sentences.tr: Alkino’, allo ti toi meletō phresin·
sentences.l: “Alcinous, something else let be a care to you in your mind;
sentences.i: “Alcinous, let something else be your concern;
sentences.n: Ἀλκίνο’ is the vocative Ἀλκίνοε elided. μελέτω is the third-person imperative of μέλω ‘be a care’, and τοι is ‘to you’ (= σοι), not the particle. φρεσίν is plural for one person’s mind, ‘in your mind’. The sentence ends in the middle of the line, and οὐ γάρ starts the reason.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ ἐγώ γε
ἀθανάτοισιν ἔοικα, τοὶ οὐρανὸν εὐρὺν ἔχουσιν,
οὐ δέμας οὐδὲ φυήν, ἀλλὰ θνητοῖσι βροτοῖσιν.
sentences.tr:
ou gar egō ge
athanatoisin eoika, toi ouranon euryn echousin,
ou demas oude phyēn, alla thnētoisi brotoisin.
sentences.l:
for I, at least, am not
like the immortals, who hold the broad heaven,
not in body nor in stature, but like mortal men.
sentences.i: for I am not like the immortals, who hold the broad heaven, in body or in stature, but like mortal men.
sentences.n: ἔοικα is the perfect ‘I am like’ with the dative; it is the verb of ἔοικε ‘it is fitting’ in 159, in another sense. τοί is the article as a relative pronoun, ‘who’. οὐ δέμας οὐδὲ φυήν are accusatives of respect: ‘not in body nor in stature’. The last words, ἀλλὰ θνητοῖσι βροτοῖσιν, have ἔοικα understood: ‘but (I am like) mortal men’. Odysseus answers the doubt Alcinous has just raised.

sentences.t:
οὕς τινας ὑμεῖς ἴστε μάλιστ’ ὀχέοντας ὀιζὺν
ἀνθρώπων, τοῖσίν κεν ἐν ἄλγεσιν ἰσωσαίμην.
sentences.tr:
hous tinas hymeis iste malist’ ocheontas oizyn
anthrōpōn, toisin ken en algesin isōsaimēn.
sentences.l:
Whichever men you know to bear most misery
of men, with them in sufferings I might rank myself equal.
sentences.i: Whichever of mankind you know to be bearing the most misery, I could match them in suffering.
sentences.n: οὕς τινας … ἀνθρώπων is the relative clause, put first, ‘whichever of men’, with τοῖσιν ‘to them’ picking it up. ἴστε is the plural of οἶδα, ‘you know’, and ὀχέοντας the participle of ὀχέω ‘bear’. ὀιζύς is ‘misery’. κεν with the optative ἰσωσαίμην is ‘I could make myself equal’; ἐν ἄλγεσιν is ‘in sufferings’.

sentences.t:
καὶ δ’ ἔτι κεν καὶ μᾶλλον ἐγὼ κακὰ μυθησαίμην,
ὅσσα γε δὴ ξύμπαντα θεῶν ἰότητι μόγησα.
sentences.tr:
kai d’ eti ken kai mallon egō kaka mythēsaimēn,
hossa ge dē xympanta theōn iotēti mogēsa.
sentences.l:
Yes, and still more evils I could tell,
as many as all together I have toiled through by the will of the gods.
sentences.i: Yes, I could tell of still more troubles, all that I have gone through by the will of the gods.
sentences.n: καὶ δ’ ἔτι κεν καὶ μᾶλλον is a cumulative phrase, ‘and moreover even more’, with κεν and the optative μυθησαίμην ‘I could tell’. ὅσσα … ξύμπαντα is ‘as many as, all together’. μόγησα is an aorist of μογέω ‘toil’, and θεῶν ἰότητι is ‘by the will of the gods’, ἰότης being ‘will, desire’.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἐμὲ μὲν δορπῆσαι ἐάσατε κηδόμενόν περ·
sentences.tr: all’ eme men dorpēsai easate kēdomenon per·
sentences.l: But me let have supper, though I am troubled;
sentences.i: But let me have my supper, troubled though I am;
sentences.n: ἐάσατε is the aorist imperative of ἐάω ‘allow’, in the second-person plural because he speaks to the whole company: ‘let me’. δορπῆσαι is the aorist infinitive of δορπέω ‘take supper’, from δόρπον, as in 166. κηδόμενον is a participle of κήδομαι ‘be troubled, distressed’, and περ ‘even though’. The reason follows, and it is the belly.

sentences.t:
οὐ γάρ τι στυγερῇ ἐπὶ γαστέρι κύντερον ἄλλο
ἔπλετο, ἥ τ’ ἐκέλευσεν ἕο μνήσασθαι ἀνάγκῃ
καὶ μάλα τειρόμενον καὶ ἐνὶ φρεσὶ πένθος ἔχοντα,
sentences.tr:
ou gar ti stygerēi epi gasteri kynteron allo
epleto, hē t’ ekeleusen heo mnēsasthai anankēi
kai mala teiromenon kai eni phresi penthos echonta,
sentences.i: For there is nothing more shameless than the hateful belly, which by sheer necessity makes a man think of it, even one who is greatly worn down and has grief in his heart,
sentences.n: κύντερον is the comparative of κύων ‘dog’, ‘more dog-like’, hence ‘more shameless, more brazen’: the literal line keeps the dog, the prose the sense. ἔπλετο is a gnomic aorist of πέλομαι, stating a general truth: ‘is’. ἥ τ’ has the epic τε of general statement. ἕο is the genitive of the pronoun, ‘of it’, with μνήσασθαι ‘to be mindful of’. ἀνάγκῃ is ‘by necessity’. τειρόμενον ‘worn down’ is the present participle of τείρω.

sentences.t:
ὡς καὶ ἐγὼ πένθος μὲν ἔχω φρεσίν, ἡ δὲ μάλ’ αἰεὶ
ἐσθέμεναι κέλεται καὶ πινέμεν, ἐκ δέ με πάντων
ληθάνει ὅσσ’ ἔπαθον, καὶ ἐνιπλησθῆναι ἀνώγει.
sentences.tr:
hōs kai egō penthos men echō phresin, hē de mal’ aiei
esthemenai keletai kai pinemen, ek de me pantōn
lēthanei hoss’ epathon, kai eniplēsthēnai anōgei.
sentences.l:
as I too have grief in my heart, and it very much always
bids me eat and drink, and out of all things makes me
forget what I have suffered, and urges me to be filled.
sentences.i: So it is with me: I have grief in my heart, but the belly is always bidding me eat and drink, and makes me forget all that I have suffered, and urges me to be filled.
sentences.n: ὡς is ‘so, just as’, tying the general truth to his own case. ἡ is the pronoun ‘she’, the belly. ἐσθέμεναι and πινέμεν are infinitives in -έμεναι and -έμεν, ‘to eat’ and ‘to drink’. ἐκ … ληθάνει is tmesis: ληθάνω is ‘make forget’, with the genitive πάντων, ‘of all that’. ἔπαθον is ‘I suffered’, and ἐνιπλησθῆναι the aorist passive infinitive, ‘to be filled’.

sentences.t:
ὑμεῖς δ’ ὀτρύνεσθαι ἅμ’ ἠοῖ φαινομένηφιν,
ὥς κ’ ἐμὲ τὸν δύστηνον ἐμῆς ἐπιβήσετε πάτρης
καί περ πολλὰ παθόντα·
sentences.tr:
hymeis d’ otrynesthai ham’ ēoi phainomenēphin,
hōs k’ eme ton dystēnon emēs epibēsete patrēs
kai per polla pathonta·
sentences.i: But you, bestir yourselves when dawn appears, so that you may set me, wretched as I am, on my fatherland, even though I have suffered much;
sentences.n: ὀτρύνεσθαι is an infinitive doing the work of an imperative, ‘bestir yourselves’. ἠοῖ φαινομένηφιν is ‘with dawn appearing’: ἠοῖ is a dative, and φαινομένηφιν has the -φιν ending. ὥς κ’ … ἐπιβήσετε is ‘so that you will set me on’, ἐπιβαίνω in its causative sense, with the genitive ἐμῆς πάτρης. τὸν δύστηνον is ‘the wretched one’, and καί περ ‘even though’. The unit ends in the middle of line 224, at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
ἰδόντα με καὶ λίποι αἰὼν
κτῆσιν ἐμήν, δμῶάς τε καὶ ὑψερεφὲς μέγα δῶμα.
sentences.tr:
idonta me kai lipoi aiōn
ktēsin emēn, dmōas te kai hypserephes mega dōma.
sentences.l:
may life leave me, once I have seen
my possessions, my maidservants, and my high-roofed great house.”
sentences.i: then let life leave me, once I have seen my possessions, my maids, and my great high-roofed house.”
sentences.n: ἰδόντα με is ‘me having seen’, an aorist participle in the accusative like με, and the subject of λίποι ‘may (it) leave’ is αἰών ‘life’: a wish, the aorist optative. καί ‘and then’ links the seeing to the death he is content to have after it. δμῶάς is ‘maidservants’, the women who serve in a household; κτῆσις is ‘possessions’; ὑψερεφές is ‘high-roofed’, of a δῶμα, and μέγα ‘great’.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἱ δ’ ἄρα πάντες ἐπῄνεον ἠδ’ ἐκέλευον
πεμπέμεναι τὸν ξεῖνον, ἐπεὶ κατὰ μοῖραν ἔειπεν.
sentences.tr:
hōs ephath’, hoi d’ ara pantes epēineon ēd’ ekeleuon
pempemenai ton xeinon, epei kata moiran eeipen.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and they then all praised it and urged
that the stranger be sent, since according to what is fitting he had spoken.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they all applauded and urged that the stranger be sent on his way, since he had spoken as was fitting.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφαθ’ is ‘so he spoke’, with ἔφαθ’ the elided imperfect ἔφατο of φημί. ἐπῄνεον is the imperfect of ἐπαινέω ‘approve, praise’. πεμπέμεναι is an infinitive in -έμεναι, ‘to send’, after ἐκέλευον ‘urged’: they urge that the stranger be sent home. κατὰ μοῖραν is ‘according to what is fitting’, from μοῖρα ‘due portion’. ἔειπεν is the epic aorist of εἶπον.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ σπεῖσάν τ’ ἔπιον θ’ ὅσον ἤθελε θυμός,
οἱ μὲν κακκείοντες ἔβαν οἶκόνδε ἕκαστος,
sentences.tr:
autar epei speisan t’ epion th’ hoson ēthele thymos,
hoi men kakkeiontes eban oikonde hekastos,
sentences.l:
But when they had poured libations and drunk, as much as their heart wished,
they, to lie down going, each one went to his own house,
sentences.i: But when they had poured libations and drunk as much as their hearts wished, the others each went off home to bed,
sentences.n: The first line is the same stock line as in 184. κακκείοντες is κατακείοντες with the middle syllables lost, ‘wishing to lie down’, a participle of a verb with the -ειω ending of desire; the English means they went home meaning to sleep. ἔβαν is the epic aorist of βαίνω, ‘they went’, and οἶκόνδε ‘homewards’ has the -δε ending of direction. ἕκαστος ‘each’ is singular, agreeing with the plural subject in sense.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὁ ἐν μεγάρῳ ὑπελείπετο δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς,
πὰρ δέ οἱ Ἀρήτη τε καὶ Ἀλκίνοος θεοειδὴς
ἥσθην·
sentences.tr:
autar ho en megarōi hypeleipeto dios Odysseus,
par de hoi Arētē te kai Alkinoos theoeidēs
hēsthēn·
sentences.i: but heavenly Odysseus was left behind in the hall, and beside him sat Arete and Alcinous, godlike in form;
sentences.n: ὑπελείπετο is the imperfect passive of ὑπολείπω ‘leave behind’. πὰρ … ἥσθην is tmesis: ‘sat beside’. ἥσθην is a dual, ‘the two of them sat’, the imperfect of ἧμαι, with the subjects Arete and Alcinous. θεοειδής is ‘godlike in form’. The sentence stops at the ano teleia after ἥσθην, the first word of line 232, and the servants’ work begins a new one.

sentences.t: ἀμφίπολοι δ’ ἀπεκόσμεον ἔντεα δαιτός.
sentences.tr: amphipoloi d’ apekosmeon entea daitos.
sentences.l: and attendants cleared away the gear of the feast.
sentences.i: and the attendants cleared away the gear of the feast.
sentences.n: ἀμφίπολοι is the plural of ἀμφίπολος, the servant of 172 (where the shipped wording ‘handmaid’ stands); the plural is ‘attendants’, the house rendering. ἀπεκόσμεον is the imperfect of ἀποκοσμέω ‘clear away, put in order’, with the open ending -εον (Attic -ουν). ἔντεα is ‘gear, implements’, and δαιτός the genitive of δαίς ‘feast’. While the servants work, Odysseus sits on with Arete and Alcinous beside him.

sentences.t: τοῖσιν δ’ Ἀρήτη λευκώλενος ἤρχετο μύθων·
sentences.tr: toisin d’ Arētē leukōlenos ērcheto mythōn·
sentences.l: and among them white-armed Arete began the talk:
sentences.i: Then white-armed Arete began to speak among them:
sentences.n: λευκώλενος ‘white-armed’ is the queen’s standing epithet and is translated every time. ἤρχετο μύθων is ‘began the talk’; ἄρχομαι governs the genitive μύθων. τοῖσιν is a dative plural, ‘among them’. There is no verb of speaking; ‘began the talk’ does its work.

sentences.t:
ἔγνω γὰρ φᾶρός τε χιτῶνά τε εἵματ’ ἰδοῦσα
καλά, τά ῥ’ αὐτὴ τεῦξε σὺν ἀμφιπόλοισι γυναιξί·
sentences.tr:
egnō gar pharos te chitōna te heimat’ idousa
kala, ta rh’ autē teuxe syn amphipoloisi gynaixi·
sentences.l:
for she recognised, both cloak and tunic, the clothes, having seen them,
fine ones, which herself she had made with her attendant women;
sentences.i: for she recognised the cloak and tunic when she saw the fine clothes, which she herself had made with her attendant women;
sentences.n: γάρ gives the reason: the clothes are hers. ἔγνω is the aorist of γιγνώσκω ‘recognise’, and εἵματ’ ἰδοῦσα is ‘having seen the clothes’, with φᾶρος ‘cloak’ and χιτών ‘tunic’ in apposition. καλά ‘fine’ belongs to εἵματα. τά ῥ’ is the relative ‘which’ (ῥ’ = ῥα). αὐτή ‘herself’ is intensive, and τεῦξε the unaugmented aorist of τεύχω ‘make’. σὺν ἀμφιπόλοισι γυναιξί is ‘with attendant women’.

sentences.t: καί μιν φωνήσασ’ ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.tr: kai min phōnēsas’ epea pteroenta prosēuda·
sentences.l: and, lifting her voice, to him winged words she spoke:
sentences.i: and, raising her voice, she spoke winged words to him:
sentences.n: καί μιν … προσηύδα is a stock line: μιν is ‘him’, φωνήσασ’ (φωνήσασα) is the aorist participle of φωνέω, ‘raising her voice’, and ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα is ‘spoke winged words’, the words flying from speaker to hearer. προσηύδα is the imperfect of προσαυδάω ‘speak to’. The ano teleia announces her question.

sentences.t: ξεῖνε, τὸ μέν σε πρῶτον ἐγὼν εἰρήσομαι αὐτή·
sentences.tr: xeine, to men se prōton egōn eirēsomai autē·
sentences.l: “Stranger, this first I will ask you, I myself:
sentences.i: “Stranger, this is what I myself shall ask you first:
sentences.n: ξεῖνε is ‘stranger’, in the vocative. τὸ μέν is ‘this, on the one hand’. εἰρήσομαι is the future of εἴρομαι ‘ask’ (= ἐρέομαι). ἐγών is the epic ἐγώ, and αὐτή ‘myself’ is feminine, so the queen stresses that she asks in her own person, not through her husband.

sentences.t: τίς πόθεν εἰς ἀνδρῶν;
sentences.tr: tis pothen eis andrōn;
sentences.l: Who among men are you, and from where?
sentences.i: Who among men are you, and where from?
sentences.n: εἰς here is the verb ‘you are’ (= Attic εἶ), not the preposition εἰς ‘into’. τίς is ‘who’, and πόθεν ‘from where’, with the -θεν suffix of direction from. ἀνδρῶν is a genitive of the whole, ‘among men’, that is, of what people or family. The first question ends at the Greek question mark in the middle of the line.

sentences.t: τίς τοι τάδε εἵματ’ ἔδωκεν;
sentences.tr: tis toi tade heimat’ edōken;
sentences.l: Who gave you these clothes?
sentences.i: Who gave you these clothes?
sentences.n: τοι is ‘to you’ (= σοι) again, not the particle. τάδε εἵματ’ is ‘these clothes’, εἵματα elided, the same word as in 234. ἔδωκεν is the aorist of δίδωμι, ‘gave’. This is the question her recognition of the clothes has been leading up to.

sentences.t: οὐ δὴ φῆς ἐπὶ πόντον ἀλώμενος ἐνθάδ’ ἱκέσθαι;
sentences.tr: ou dē phēs epi ponton alōmenos enthad’ hikesthai;
sentences.l: Do you not indeed say that over the open-sea wandering you have come here?”
sentences.i: Do you not say that you came here wandering over the sea?”
sentences.n: οὐ δὴ φῆς is a question that expects yes, ‘do you not indeed say’. ἀλώμενος is the present participle of ἀλάομαι ‘wander’, and πόντον ‘open sea’ is accusative after ἐπί. ἱκέσθαι is the aorist infinitive, ‘to have come’, after φῆς. The last question asks him to confirm that he came by sea, and it closes her speech.
